bet.text: Keep the center of gravity very low: a pivoting elevator keeps all motors and frame, apart from light forks, under about 14 inches from the ground when fully stowed.

demand.text: The team wanted a wide touch-it-own-it intake, a fast and reliable autonomous balance because balancing counts toward a ranking point, and a climb that takes little space on the charge station.

auto.text: In build season the team worked on a fast, reliable automatic balance, starting with a gyroscope on the previous year's robot and then trying wheel-speed and vision measurements. Its Beta robot balanced for the first time in week 6.
Autos ran on dead reckoning, without vision, at no more than about 3.5 m/s.

cycle.text: LEDs show the human player whether a cone or cube is wanted. The player drops cones so they land upright in front of the station; the robot grabs one and leaves. The operator picks a node on the D-pad and the robot prepares to score there.

endgame.text: Forks bolted to the arm lift only the drive base, because the elevator drops with them. The idea came from 2019 buddy climbs in which forks slid under a partner let a robot hang off the edge.

fallback.text: In a Galileo final a commentator describes the collector breaking: the robot tried two cubes and a cone, then switched to defense and kept its off-the-side climb.
A spare intake was ready, but swapping meant de-soldering, and the spare came off the practice robot with similar wear, so the same plate might snap mid-match.

gave_up.text: The team skipped a steel belly pan to stay light. It says the robot did not often rise onto two wheels, except when going to load at the human-player shelf.

changed.text: Two early ideas for hanging off the charge station, a roller bar and wooden blocks, failed from friction and lack of weight.

Carbon-fiber intake cross beams snapped at earlier regionals and let the intake tilt, so aluminum replaced them. The forks were shortened for the championship, which made lining up and climbing on both sides easier.

outcome.text: 62-7-1 in official play; won the Galileo division; captain of the Galileo alliance on Einstein; ranked 10 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 75.28, Galileo).

facts.text: 26 in by 26 in frame with MK4i swerve modules
Team page names agility as a main focus
Joystick speeds pass through a filtering step that keeps the robot stable when the elevator is extended
Rotational acceleration is limited when the robot is tall; translational acceleration is not, mostly by driver preference, because a limit made small adjustments less snappy
The team runs one set of black neoprene tread per event

cost.text: Impacts bent or tore drivetrain tubes, so the side rails changed to 1/8 in wall tubing

functions.name: Low center of gravity layout

solves.text: Avoid tipping and stay consistent in every match by keeping everything as low as possible

functions.type: motors and battery kept low, light robot

facts.text: Inspected weight at the championship, without battery and bumpers
Battery mounted toward the back, low and close to the arm's pivot
Falcon 500 motors stay near the belly pan, except the wrist and rollers
Unpocketed belly pan across the top and bottom of the rails
High-strength rivets, with about double the shear and tensile strength, go in the drive frame, belly pan and other high-load areas, about 10 percent of rivets in a typical year

cost.text: High-strength rivets cost $0.15 to $0.25 each and are annoying to drill out, because the shank snaps inside

functions.name: Pivoting elevator

solves.text: Reach all three rows while everything is powered as low as possible

functions.type: continuous three-stage elevator on a pivoting arm

facts.text: Reaches all three rows
Sliding structure uses MAXTube and WCP bearing blocks
String guards, including one in the tensioner, replace a grooved spool so the center spool stays rigid
Arm gearbox is custom on a MAXPlanetary, with gears shimmed against backlash
The week 7 build blog says the first competition robot's new elevator would use chains instead of belts, while the championship interview describes strings
Rope is tied to small spacers fixed to the spool
Team 341's 2025 binder credits this robot's elevator as the inspiration for its spool
Rope is 1/8 in Spectra or Dyneema
The raising and lowering ropes wind on the same spool in opposite directions, so one tightens as the other loosens
A spring in the rope absorbs shock and keeps it tight; the rope runs at an angle, so its tension would otherwise change as the elevator moves
The string guards make each wrap lie beside the last, so one turn of the spool always moves the same length of rope
Nothing controls which stage moves first
The arm pivots on a 1 in ceramic-coated 6061 aluminum shaft; critical bores are machined about 0.010 in undersize and then reamed
Shim tape on 3 of the 6 faces of the main joint's hex shaft reduces gear wiggle
Arm gearbox reduction, about
The thin 2x1 elevator tubes had no major bending problem, likely because the load falls on their reinforced corners
The alpha robot's fixed arm of about 6 ft was hard to drive with; the team says it learned little else from that robot

cost.text: The rope stretched during the season, so knots were untied, pulled tight and retied
The spool sits at a slant to the pulleys, so string came off early on, until U-shaped printed string guards were added
Without upper braces the tubes spread until bearing blocks lost contact, and shifted into a parallelogram; added braces pull the tubes slightly inward
The wire chain sometimes snapped, usually because of something else such as an elevator failure or a collision

functions.name: Wrist

solves.text: Drive the wrist from a distance so the center of gravity stays low

functions.type: chain-driven wrist with its motor lower in the arm

facts.text: A gearbox set away from the wrist drives it through chain, to keep the center of gravity low
The elevator let the team keep the wrist motor lower in the arm and route chain to the last stage

functions.name: Intake

solves.text: Pick up both pieces from a wide zone with one ground position

functions.type: wide roller intake based on the Everybot design

facts.text: Cones pass through the top two rollers and cubes through the bottom jaw
Three polycarbonate rollers with layered silicone; the back one holds a cube and the front two pick up upright cones
When the bottom bar touches the ground, one preset works for both pieces
About seven full iterations
Aluminum cross bars, with polycarbonate at the bottom to stay light
End-roller stack: bolt through the plate, spacer, two bearings, nut; inspired by 254's rollers of the year before
The end spacer is PLA with a slight cone, so it bears on the plate but misses the bearing's outer race
Roller end inserts are Markforged Onyx; the printed roller pulleys have axial layers, so the through-bolt holds most of the print in compression
The silicone sleeve has a 1.375 in inside diameter and is floated with compressed air onto a 2 in roller
Polycord loops are cut to the path length minus 5 to 10 percent

cost.text: At the championship the polycarbonate side plates fractured on impact, one on each side, at the 2x1 tube that passes through them, where the least material was; the team thinks wear was the likely cause and that swapping them beforehand would likely have prevented it
Swapping the intake means de-soldering connections, which the team avoids at events; in retrospect it could likely have kept the motor and swapped the rest
Another reply says only the CAN wires were soldered, and power extensions used connectors

A version with two round carbon tubes clamped by printed blocks was light, but the side plates twisted and could stick, so the front roller passed over cone tips; heavier, stiffer tubes and gussets fixed it
Square nuts sometimes stripped their slots in the printed roller pulleys; raising infill to 45 percent worked much better than adding walls
Getting that sleeve onto the roller is hard; a 2024 post says tubing sized closer to the roller is much easier

solves.text: Climb while taking up little space on the charge station

facts.text: No separate motor, wiring or control, because they bolt to the arm
Only the drive base of the roughly 90 lb robot is lifted
Shortened for the championship by about
A commentator says the off-the-side climb let the robot play longer before climbing than an opponent could
Carbon fiber tube length in the team's pit display text
The formed 0.0625 in sheet part around each carbon tube has a rubber layer, about 1/16 in, which grips and avoids point loads that would crack the tube

cost.text: The longer forks were difficult to line up, especially on the side near the wall

functions.name: Human player LEDs and node selection

solves.text: Get in and out of the loading zone as soon as possible

facts.text: LEDs tell the human player whether the robot wants a cone or a cube
The operator picks a node on the D-pad and the scoring position updates to match

functions.name: Alignment without vision

solves.text: Line up with scoring locations; the build blog wanted this automatic

functions.type: dead reckoning in auto, manual alignment in teleop

facts.text: In week 1 the team planned to use AprilTags to line up with scoring spots and to support autonomous where wheel odometry suffers
Beta used a three-camera setup in week 5; the first competition robot got new Limelight sensors in week 7
Two team posts after the season say the robot used no vision: dead reckoning in auto and manual alignment in teleop
Auto path speeds started at 2 m/s, and five successful runs in a row was the cue to move on
In season, paths were shimmed to account for wheel odometry error

functions.name: Bumper mounts
functions.type: studs fixed to the bumper wood, held by flange nuts

facts.text: A 1/4-20 stud with a flat four-hole head goes through the bumper wood, held by wood screws; a flanged locknut clamps it in a bracket on the frame
Nuts are reused within a competition and swapped when the nylon wears out

cost.text: Pockets drilled too deep or bolts overtightened can make the nuts hard to loosen

decisions.because: a mid-build-season switch was too much scope for the students and had trade-offs the team did not like

the team had more experience with classic elevators and there are more robust off-the-shelf parts; it also keeps the wrist motor lower in the arm. The post adds that 2910 probably built a similar robot much better
it needs fewer strings and is less complicated, so there are fewer failure modes; it is already violent enough that cascade rigging would only add complexity

decisions.choice: No ballast in the belly pan
decisions.because: staying light helps acceleration, deceleration and battery draw, and the ballast turned out not to be needed
carbon-fiber beams snapped and were not rigid enough

decisions.choice: Bolt the climbing forks to the arm
decisions.because: it adds no separate motor, wiring, control or weight

decisions.choice: Leave most fasteners out of CAD
decisions.because: even simplified fasteners added a lot of load time; only tight clearances get one or two
it keeps the center of gravity as low as possible while crossing the field, and gave the climbing forks basically for free
decisions.instead_of: a static elevator at an angle

decisions.choice: Lower the pivot and add an extension stage
decisions.because: it gained on center of gravity
decisions.instead_of: the first-week layout shared with the alpha robot

decisions.because: the team has long experience with it, and it is strong and flexible to route
its angle changes continuously through a match

decisions.choice: Second 5:1 stage in the arm gearbox
decisions.because: a single 5:1 was not enough to keep the robot up after the endgame lift
they weigh a lot less; many of these joints would need 2 in bolts, a lot of steel far out on the elevator
it is easier to wire, program, inventory and design when every motor that matters is the same
decisions.instead_of: a smaller motor such as a NEO 550

decisions.because: a sheet timing each cone and cube cycle was a burden to practice with and was abandoned
